models.approach: Argue that a feed is not evidence of job performance, and that using it imports every bias it contains.
plan: Introduction: state the position and the standard you will judge by.
Body 1: what a social media profile actually reveals.
Body 2: concede the legitimate cases, then bound them.
Conclusion: the rule you would prefer.

paras.text: Employers can now read a decade of somebody's opinions before meeting them, and the question is whether that is information or merely material. [[In my opinion]] it is mostly the latter, and permitting it as a hiring criterion would make recruitment less accurate rather than more.

[[The main point is]] that a feed reveals age, religion, politics, pregnancy and health, which are the exact categories employers are forbidden to consider. Looking at it does not make a manager biased, but it supplies everything bias needs, and the resulting decision is [[irreproachable]] on paper because no one has to say why. [[There is evidence that]] identical applications with different profiles attached receive markedly different callback rates.

[[Granted]], some checks are reasonable. A public post inciting violence, or one leaking a former employer's confidential material, is [[germane]] to whether somebody should be hired, and no employer should ignore it. [[That said]], those are narrow and specific, whereas the practice at issue is a general trawl through a person's private life. [[It is worth noting]] that the material is also poor evidence: a joke from age nineteen predicts almost nothing about a thirty-year-old's work.

[[In conclusion]], I disagree with a general permission while accepting narrow exceptions. Employers should be allowed to consider public professional conduct and nothing else, since anything wider imports the [[insidious]] kind of discrimination that the law can no longer see.

notes: Naming the protected categories in body one is what turns a privacy objection into a legal and practical one.
The concession is genuine and specific, and the conclusion then writes it into the rule. That is how a concession earns its place.
A joke from age nineteen is the concrete detail that makes the accuracy argument land.

models.approach: Argue that public speech is public, and that employers already bear the consequences of it.
plan: Introduction: agree, with the distinction between public and private.
Body 1: why public conduct is legitimately relevant.
Body 2: concede the discrimination risk, then answer with process.
Conclusion: restate, with the safeguards that make it acceptable.

paras.text: A public post is a statement made to the world, not a diary entry read over somebody's shoulder. [[On the whole]] I agree that employers may consider it, provided the material is genuinely public and genuinely relevant.

[[First and foremost]], employers carry the consequences of their staff's public conduct. A hospital whose new nurse has been publicly mocking patients, or a school whose teacher posts abuse, will answer for it, and pretending the material does not exist is [[injudicious]] rather than principled. [[It is clear that]] the same applies to a candidate whose feed shows they have repeatedly published a previous employer's confidential information: that is a demonstrated [[propensity]], not a guess.

[[It must be acknowledged]] that the practice invites discrimination. A profile discloses religion, politics and family circumstances, and the risk that these influence a decision is real. [[Nevertheless]], the remedy is procedure rather than prohibition: a documented search conducted by somebody outside the hiring panel, limited to public posts and recorded in writing, keeps the relevant material and makes the [[impartial]] handling of it auditable.

[[All things considered]], I agree that employers should be permitted this, on conditions. Public accounts only, a written record, no fishing through friends and family, and a right for the candidate to respond would preserve the legitimate use while making the [[insidious]] one much harder to hide.

notes: The strongest version of this position is procedural: it accepts the danger and designs against it rather than denying it.
The hospital and the school are examples where nobody would defend ignoring the material, which is what makes the general permission plausible.
The conclusion lists four safeguards. A conditional agreement needs its conditions written out, not gestured at.

models.approach: Draw the line at what the candidate published in a professional capacity, and defend that line on both accuracy and fairness.
plan: Introduction: the question is too broad; propose the line.
Body 1: why professional output is fair to consider.
Body 2: why the rest is neither fair nor useful.
Conclusion: the rule, and why it is enforceable.

paras.text: Social media activity covers a published article and a photograph from a wedding, and treating them as one category is what makes this argument unresolvable. [[To a certain extent]] I agree with employer access, but only to what a candidate published as a professional.

Where somebody has written publicly about their field, the material is both relevant and volunteered. A developer's public code, a designer's portfolio and a consultant's published essays are offered precisely so that others may judge them, and reading them is no different from reading a reference. [[It is evident that]] such work is often better evidence than an interview, since it shows the candidate's judgement at length rather than their composure for an hour.

[[By contrast]], a personal account is neither offered as evidence nor useful as it. It reveals protected characteristics, it is frequently misread out of context, and a decade-old post is a poor guide to a present adult. [[Not surprisingly]], the practice also has a chilling effect: people learn to say nothing anywhere, which is an [[intrusion]] into ordinary life that no hiring gain justifies.

[[On balance]], then, employers should read what a candidate published professionally and leave the rest alone. The line is [[explicit]] enough to be written into a policy and to be audited afterwards, which is more than can be said for any rule that asks recruiters to look but not to be influenced.

notes: The distinction between volunteered professional output and a personal account resolves a question that is otherwise a clash of principles.
The chilling effect argument extends the harm beyond the individual candidate, which broadens the essay without loosening it.
Arguing that the line is enforceable is the practical test, and it is what makes the position more than a preference.
